headline: HPCL is increasingly buying Middle Eastern crude ​on a delivered basis due to freight discounts - The HinduBusinessLine
summary_text: India's state-run Hindustan Petroleum Corp is increasingly buying Middle Eastern crude ​on a delivered basis, as producers with stranded cargoes offer ‌discounts to offset higher freight costs, its ​chair said on Friday. The refiner directly operates ⁠three refineries with a combined capacity of 670,000 barrels per day. "For all practical purposes right now almost everything ‌we are looking at is on landed basis except where we think we can send ‌a ship and pick it up cheaper," ‌said ⁠Vikas Kaushal on an analyst call after HPCL's ⁠September-quarter earnings. Supply disruptions from the Middle East, as the Iran war enters its eighth month, have pushed Asian refiners to ​buy spot Middle Eastern oil ‌on a delivered basis. Attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have also tightened shipping availability and driven freight rates close to record highs. Freight ‌rates doubled in July to September from ​the previous quarter, HPCL finance chief Srividya Venkataraman said. The cost of shipping crude on ⁠a Suezmax tanker has risen to about $9 per barrel from $3 to $4 in the June quarter, she said. "The ‌impact on landed prices might not be as much as you guys think from outside because the producers of oil are also stuck," Kaushal said, adding that returns to producers with stranded cargoes were much lower than publicly reported. He said delivered ‌cargoes previously accounted for about half of HPCL's crude imports. The ​company is increasingly opting for delivered cargoes to avoid exposing its own vessels to attacks ⁠and other risks linked to the regional conflict. Kaushal also ⁠said HPCL expects to start producing high-sulphur fuel oil at its 180,000-bpd Rajasthan refinery ‌in December. The refinery is operating at 60 per cent capacity and is expected to reach full capacity by ​end-December or early January, he said.

headline: HPCL's Debt Refinancing for Rajasthan Refinery: A Game-Changer with Rs 1,000 Crore Annual Savings, ETEnergyworld
summary_text: New Delhi: Hindustan Petroleum Corp. (HPCL) has refinanced about ₹50,000 crore of debt at its Rajasthan refinery, securing a reduction of around 105 basis points in borrowing costs and targeting annual interest savings of about ₹1,000 crore through a broader restructuring of the project's finances, Chairman and Managing Director Vikas Kaushal said on Friday. The refinancing, effective October 3, is expected to save the company about ₹470 crore to ₹550 crore annually, Kaushal told analysts on an earnings call. Additional equity infusions, conversion of subordinated loans into equity and interest-free state support are expected to further ease the refinery's financing burden as HPCL ramps up operations at the facility. ... The 9 million tonnes a year refinery in Rajasthan was built at a cost of ₹79,459 crore, with HPCL (74 per cent) and Government of Rajasthan (26 per cent) as equity partners. HPCL Rajasthan Refinery Limited (HRRL), the joint venture company, part refinanced existing project loans through ₹8,000 crore in rupee term loans from a consortium comprising the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID), India Infrastructure Finance Company Limited (IIFCL), ICICI Bank Limited, UCO Bank and Punjab & Sind Bank; a ₹2,000 crore working capital demand loan from Bank of Baroda; and fund-based and non-fund-based credit facilities aggregating to ₹400 crore from ICICI Bank Limited. ... The term loan proceeds will be utilised for the part refinancing of existing project loans, while the working capital facilities will support HRRL's working capital requirements and help address cash flow mismatches associated with the project, including its allied utilities and facilities at Pachpadra, District Balotra, Rajasthan. Kaushal said the financial restructuring is aimed at improving the economics of the Rajasthan refinery, a major new asset that HPCL expects to bring towards full operating capacity by December. The company is also working to stabilise its other complex refining assets and contain costs as volatile crude prices and rising losses on domestic cooking gas threaten near-term earnings. ... "We have significantly altered the debt structure of the company," he said, adding that the refinancing and other measures could reduce annual interest costs by about ₹1,000 crore compared with the previous year. The Rajasthan government infused ₹1,500 crore of equity into the refinery during the September quarter, while HPCL converted ₹4,300 crore of subordinated loans into equity, Kaushal said. The conversion is expected to lower interest costs by about ₹350 crore. Further equity calls are planned over the next one or two quarters. The state has also committed to providing about ₹1,100 crore annually in interest-free loans, with the first instalment already received, according to Kaushal. HPCL is seeking to improve the refinery's financial performance as it moves beyond commissioning and begins shipping substantial volumes of products. The facility's commercial operation date was declared on June 22 and it is currently running at about 60 per cent utilisation, broadly in line with earlier guidance. Almost all secondary processing units are operating in hot circulation, with two units still to be brought into that state. HPCL expects to complete the remaining commissioning work, including the sulphur recovery unit, before moving towards full-capacity operations. The company expects throughput to reach a run rate of 8 million to 9 million tonnes per annum around December, give or take a week or two, Kaushal said. The refinery recorded a gross refining margin of about $12 per barrel in the September quarter. HPCL expects margins to rise above $20 per barrel in the fourth quarter as it transitions to processing higher-sulphur crude, which the facility is designed to handle. Product shipments have already increased sharply. Kaushal said the refinery shipped about 15,000 tonnes of products on the day before the call, compared with no shipments three months earlier. October shipments are expected to exceed 400,000 tonnes, generating revenue of more than ₹4,000 crore for the month. Kaushal said the refinery could post a positive monthly profit before tax in October, although he stressed that this was an expression of management's optimism rather than formal guidance, given the volatility of refining margins and the early stage of operations. "We are very excited on the Rajasthan. We are very bullish on it," he said.

Revenue from operations rose 26.1% YoY to Rs 1,39,140 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 1,10,323 crore in Q2FY26. For the first half of FY27 (H1FY27), revenue from operations increased to Rs 2,84,267 crore from Rs 2,30,458 crore in the corresponding period last year. **Gross refining margins surge** HPCL's gross refining margin (GRM) before export cess rose to $32.15 per barrel in Q2FY27, compared with $8.80 per barrel in Q2FY26. ### Live Events For H1FY27, GRM before export cess stood at $27.89 per barrel, up from $5.95 per barrel in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year. **Refining throughput remains strong** HPCL's refineries processed 6.20 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil during Q2FY27, operating at 100% of their combined capacity. The Visakh Refinery processed 3.60 MMT of crude oil at 95% capacity utilisation, while the Mumbai Refinery processed 2.60 MMT, operating at 109% of capacity. During H1FY27, the company's refineries recorded a cumulative crude throughput of 12.72 MMT, operating at 104% of capacity. Combined petrol and diesel sales rose 9% to 16.55 MMT during the first half. Total LPG sales stood at 3.76 MMT, while pipeline throughput reached 13.83 MMT. **Capital expenditure and infrastructure expansion** HPCL incurred capital expenditure of Rs 2,085 crore in Q2FY27, taking cumulative capex for H1FY27 to Rs 3,819 crore. The investments were directed towards strengthening refining and marketing infrastructure and improving operational efficiency. HPCL Rajasthan Refinery Ltd (HRRL) received an upgrade in its long-term credit rating to AA+ from AA, with a stable outlook, from CRISIL Ratings. The company also refinanced or repriced debt arrangements worth Rs 51,970 crore with lenders at a lower cost. During the quarter, HPCL mechanically completed the 201-km LPG pipeline from Haldia to Panagarh in West Bengal. The pipeline is currently in the pre-commissioning stage. The company also commissioned an open-access fuel farm facility at Bhogapuram Airport and commenced refuelling operations. **Retail network expands** As of September 30, 2026, HPCL operated 25,245 retail outlets and 6,394 LPG distributorships. Its piped natural gas (PNG) network had 77,984 connections. Under its retail energy transition initiatives, the company had 2,296 compressed natural gas (CNG) outlets and 5,880 electric vehicle (EV) charging stations as of September 30, 2026. HPCL had also solarised 24,172 retail outlets, accounting for 96% of its network. **New initiatives and green energy push** HPCL's EBITDA improvement programme, Project Samriddhi 2.0, generated accruals of Rs 327 crore during H1FY27, equivalent to $0.18 per barrel, according to the company. The HP Green R&D Centre (HPGRDC) had filed a cumulative 800 patents as of September 30, 2026, of which 339 had been granted. During the quarter, HPCL commissioned India's first refinery blue hydrogen unit at its Visakh Refinery. The unit is based on patented Higas technology and HP Novel Amine. The company also launched HP Navya, a 10-kg composite LPG cylinder, and partnered with Swiggy Instamart to enter the quick-commerce segment. It had released 0.36 lakh new connections up to September 2026. In its lubricants business, HPCL expanded its international presence with sales in Turkey and Sudan, taking its footprint to 35 countries worldwide. On the green energy front, HP Renewable & Green Energy Ltd secured consent to establish for nine compressed biogas (CBG) projects from state pollution control boards. It also secured awards for four municipal solid waste-based projects from urban local bodies in Punjab and Bihar. Additionally, the company obtained Central Electricity Authority approval for its 70 MWp Gaaliveedu Solar Project. **HPCL share price** Shares of HPCL ended Thursday’s trading session at Rs 340.80 on the NSE, down 1.87% from the previous close of Rs 347.30. headline: HPCL swings to ₹3,483 crore profit in Q2, beats estimates on operating earnings - CNBC TV18
summary_text: ## Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd reported a net profit of ₹3,482.6 crore for the July-September quarter, recovering from a loss in the previous quarter. Revenue from operations reached around ₹1.3 lakh crore, and gross refining margins improved to $27.89 per barrel. HPCL also recognized LPG compe... headline: India base oil capacity to grow as CPCL, HPCL projects advance - F&L Asia
summary_text: A foundation stone in Chennai, India, and an engineering contract in Mumbai, India, have brought two base oil expansions a step closer. Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) laid the foundation stone on October 11 for a Group II/III plant, and Technip Energies announced on October 12 that Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) had awarded it a contract for major units in its Mumbai lube modernisation project. Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid the foundation stone remotely for CPCL’s Group II/III lube oil base stocks (LOBS) project at its Manali refinery in Chennai, India, CPCL said. The project will have a planned production capacity of 270,000 tonnes per year, Projects Monitor reported, and will make base stocks used in premium-quality lubricants. The publication added that it is expected to reduce reliance on base oil imports and strengthen India’s manufacturing capabilities. CPCL said the project involves an investment of INR 16.2 billion (USD 170.7 million) and is scheduled for completion in October 2028. Engineers India Limited (EIL) will execute the project on an engineering, procurement and construction management (EPCM) basis, and construction is expected to generate about 9 million direct and indirect work hours, the company said. ... In Mumbai, Technip Energies has been awarded a large engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract by HPCL for its Lube Modernization and Bottom Upgradation (LMBU) project at the Mumbai Refinery in Maharashtra, India, the company said on October 12. The contract covers a 550,000 tonnes per year integrated hydrocracker and catalytic dewaxing unit and an 850,000 tonnes per year solvent deasphalting unit, which will be integrated within the operating refinery, according to Technip Energies. The LMBU project will lift the refinery’s lube oil base stock capacity to 764,000 tonnes per year from 475,000 tonnes per year, an increase of 289,000 tonnes per year, HPCL said in a January 2025 press release filed with the stock exchanges. The additional output will be Group II+ and Group III base oils. The project will also raise bitumen production by about 487,000 tonnes per year, according to the release. HPCL originally put the project cost at INR 46.79 billion (USD 493.2 million). Oil & Gas Journal (OGJ) reported that the cost had risen to INR 57.40 billion (USD 605.0 million) as of March 31, 2026, citing HPCL’s May 13, 2026 investor presentation. The project was 9.9% physically complete at that date, with full completion scheduled for March 2028, OGJ reported. ... Technip Energies did not disclose the contract value. It defines a large award as one representing between EUR 250 million and EUR 500 million (USD 280 million to USD 561 million) of revenue, and said the order intake will be recorded in the backlog of its Project Delivery segment in the third quarter of 2026.

headline: HPCL taps Technip Energies for EPC on new Mumbai refinery unit | Oil & Gas Journal
summary_text: Alongside raising the Mumbai refinery’s bitumen production by about 487,000 tpy, HPCL’s LMBU project will expand the complex's output of LOBS to 764,000 tpy from 475,000 tpy, including production of Group II+ and Group III base stocks. Hindustan Petroleum Corp. Ltd. (HPCL) has awarded Technip Energies an engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract for two major units in the lube modernization and bottoms upgradation (LMBU) project at its 9.5-million tonne/year (tpy) Mumbai refinery in Maharashtra, India. The work covers a 550,000-tpy integrated hydrocracker and catalytic dewaxing (IHCD) unit and an 850,000-tpy solvent deasphalting (SDA) unit. Both will be integrated into the operating refinery, Technip Energies said in a release Oct. 12. The new units aim to increase production of lube oil base stocks (LOBS) used in automotive engine oils and industrial lubricants, while upgrading heavier refinery streams into higher-value products, according to the service provider. While Technip Energies did not reveal the precise value of the contract, the company confirmed the order would amount to between €250-500 million of revenue. This latest EPC contract for the project’s IHCD and SDA units follows HPCL’s earlier award to Chevron Lummus Global for licensing of technologies to outfit the IHCD unit. ... overview HPCL’s LMBU project is designed to raise the Mumbai refinery’s output of LOBS to 764,000 tpy from 475,000 tpy, including production of Group II+ and Group III base stocks. The project is also expected to increase bitumen production by about 487,000 tpy through fuel oil upgrading, as well as improve the refinery’s yield of distillate by about 4%, HPCL said in a release Jan. 23, 2025. HPCL began work on the LMBU project during the third quarter of its 2025 fiscal year at an estimated project cost of 46.79 billion rupees (US$541.1 million). Scheduled to be fully completed in March 2028, the LMBU project had reached 9.9% physical completion as of Mar. 31, 2026, at a then-current project cost of 57.40 billion rupees (US$600.4 million), HPCL said in an investor presentation dated May 13, 2026.

headline: Visakh Refinery to get six new reactors - The Hindu
summary_text: Public oil sector major Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) has floated a high-value tender for the supply of six specialised refinery reactors at its Visakh Refinery as part of its efforts to strengthen its secondary processing facilities. According to official procurement notices on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal, the project covers the end-to-end supply, positioning, and site commissioning of the reactors, which are designed to operate under high-temperature and high-pressure parameters. Speaking to The Hindu, a senior HPCL official said: “Yes, the procurement proces is correct. Following contract award, the vendor has a strict 252-day window to complete installation and commissioning of all six reactors to boost secondary processing reliability.” The new six reactors are expected to improve operational flexibility, by allowing the refinery to process cheaper, heavier crude slates while maximising yields of high-value light distillates like petrol and diesel. The procurement follows the multi-billion-dollar Visakh Refinery Modernisation Project (VRMP), which expanded the crude processing capacity from 8.33 MMTPA to 15 MMTPA. #### Core Engineering for Clean BS-VI Fuel Mandates Industry experts say that in modern petroleum refining, such reactors play a key role in processing core for hydrotreating, hydroprocessing, and catalytic reforming operations. By utilising hydrogen streams, these specialised reactors strip sulfur, nitrogen, and heavy metal impurities from intermediate petroleum cuts, enabling the production of ultra-low-sulfur fuels compliant with strict Bharat Stage VI (BS-VI) environmental emission mandates. The bidding opened on September 25, 2026, and will close on October 15, 2026. The awarded contractor will have 252 days from contract award to complete installation and initial commissioning, supported by a 5% Performance Bank Guarantee, and Make in India purchase preferences.

headline: Electrification Can Give Us a Big Push Towards Decarbonisation - ENERGDIVE
summary_text: # Electrification Can Give Us a Big Push Towards Decarbonisation For energy-intensive industries, decarbonisation will ultimately come down to economics, reliability and scale. ENERGDIVE sat with Anshu Sharma, Vice President – Petrochemical Operations and Maintenance, HPCL-Mittal Energy Ltd (HMEL), to discuss why electrification offers a near-term opportunity, what is holding back low-carbon technologies, and how policy and digitalisation can accelerate adoption. ... A: I would look at it the other way around—which is the quickest way from that point of view? In the oil industry, we consume a lot of energy, so electrification is one of the quickest ways for us to move into this field. Considering that, until a decade ago, most of our refineries produced their own electricity, and none of them could anticipate being connected to the grid. Everybody, every refinery, had its own captive power plant, which in turn meant that we were emitting a lot of emissions because fossil fuel was being used to generate that electricity. But now, as things are progressing, let me share with you that when we built our petrochemical complex about four to six years ago, we took a decision that the grids had become more stable and we were able to get electricity on a consistent basis. So, we switched over to the grid, and that itself reduced a good amount of our carbon footprint for us. And then it is very easy. Now, as a good amount of renewable energy is being used to generate that electricity, electrification can give us a big push in this direction straight away. So, that becomes the easiest and the fastest way for us because it is a much more proven aspect. So, that is how I look at it for the big energy guzzlers like refineries and petrochemicals. ... Q: Many low-carbon technologies have demonstrated technical feasibility, but commercial scale remains elusive. What is the single biggest obstacle preventing large-scale adoption today? A: The single, large-scale hurdle is scalability. From that point of view, technology has to become reliable and economical. Refineries or plants work 24/7, seven days a week, 365 days a year, and sometimes run for years without a shutdown. So, any technology that we adopt at the plant scale and take to an industrial scale has to be reliable. At the same time, it has to create economic value. Every technology requires capital expenditure, operating expenditure, and energy, so every investment is evaluated from an economic point of view. > "Technology has to become reliable and economical. Refineries or plants work 24/7, seven days a week, 365 days a year, and sometimes run for years without a shutdown" We should also be able to deploy the technology at various locations. There should be an infrastructure around it; the vendors and trained manpower should be available, and the necessary infrastructure should be in place. If all these aspects are available for a technology, including one that has been demonstrated at the pilot scale, then we can scale it up and have the industry adopt it much faster. So, these aspects have to be taken into consideration before we move towards the adoption of any new technology. ... A: That is a beautiful question. We need a lot of support in this regard as operators. Collaboration among stakeholders is required to make these things viable. Policymakers have to provide the right incentives so that, from an economic point of view, we are able to adopt these technologies. The necessary infrastructure also needs to be developed. So, the policies have to be developed in a way that incentivises people to start adopting these technologies. These policy interventions by the government are important, whether it is for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), circular polymers, or carbon capture. Resource sharing also has to be enabled. From the circular polymer point of view, for example, waste management will require municipalities and producers to come together, and some incentives will need to be provided to them as well. These aspects have to be addressed from a policy perspective. Once that framework is in place, the movement towards adoption can become much faster. ... So, how do we make that happen? We need to create an ecosystem in which companies are incentivised to invest. That is why policy interventions by the government, whether through grants or other policy initiatives, are necessary so that industries can flourish while moving towards Net Zero.

headline: Nayara Energy shipped 1.20 lakh tonne petrol to Russia in August - The HinduBusinessLine
summary_text: Rosneft-backed Nayara Energy exported roughly 1.20 lakh tonne of petrol to Russia in August 2026 valued at around $90 million from its refinery at Vadinar in Gujarat. Moscow imported around $132 million worth of refined petroleum products last month, of which India supplied around 70 per cent or roughly $92.50 million, said a report by Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). ... On the other hand, after two consecutive months of record-high crude oil imports from Russia, India’s shipments decreased by 24 per cent in August month-on-month, CREA said. “Imports by all three of India’s largest Russian crude-importing refineries remained high in August: the Jamnagar refinery (fell 15 per cent M-o-M), Vadinar refinery (rose 5 per cent) and Paradip refinery (increased a minor 1 per cent),’’ it added. The IndianOil Vadinar SMPL installation imported a significantly lower quantity of Russian crude oil in August, down 48 per cent from the prior month. headline: HPCL-led energy fund to back deep-tech start-ups; targets to cut industry’s refining bill worth ₹1 lakh crore - The Hindu
summary_text: A band of public sector oil and gas companies, led by Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (HPCL), is setting up a deep-tech incubation and investment ecosystem aimed at solving some of the energy sector’s biggest technology challenges, including an opportunity to cut the nearly ₹1 lakh crore that India’s refining industry spends annually on energy, said HPCL Chairman and Managing Director Vikas Kaushal here on Tuesday. A consortium of oil companies have formed a Section 8 company, MC2 Plus, which would operate as an incubator and accelerator for start-ups working on deep technology for the core energy sector. The initiative would subsequently be backed by a professionally managed Alternative Investment Fund (AIF), which Mr. Kaushal described as an “India Energy Fund,” with a sizeable corpus for investing in energy-focused start-ups. The proposed fund is expected to be launched shortly, he added. ... According to Mr. Kaushal, the scale of the opportunity is particularly significant in refining. India has around 270 million tones of refining capacity, and the sector spends close to ₹1 lakh crore a year on energy used in the refining process alone. The figure does not include the energy required for transporting and distributing petroleum products. He argued that the changing energy landscape was making these challenges increasingly complex. Refiners now have multiple options for sourcing electricity and fuels, including grid power, captive generation and renewable electricity, besides conventional fuels such as gas, naphtha and fuel oil. At the same time, crude and fuel prices have become more volatile, while new fuels and technologies such as green hydrogen, energy storage and round-the-clock renewable power were emerging, he added. ... The oil and gas sector itself has been slow to tap the start-up ecosystem, he acknowledged. For instance, HPCL had invested around ₹30 crore in startups over the past six to seven years when it could actually had the ability to invest ₹3,000 crore in that same period and that was a miss the sector had,’’ he lamented. MC2 Plus was intended to address this gap by pooling the capabilities of several oil and gas companies rather than having individual companies pursue start-ups independently. HPCL would establish an incubator at its research facility in Bengaluru, Mr. Kaushal said, while other oil-sector companies are also expected to open their research infrastructure to start-ups. Mr. Kaushal said the platform would seek participation from start-ups, students, researchers and academics and urged entrepreneurs to approach the programme with solutions to real-world energy problems. “We want to create a deep-tech ecosystem in the country in the core energy domain,” he said.

headline: 印度多家石化生产商9月5日集中调整价格：Nayara与HMEL上调PP，IOCL上调PTA和MEG、下调DEG - B910化工
summary_text: 9月5日消息，据印度聚合物市场资讯平台Polymerupdate当日发布的定价快讯，印度国内市场多家石化生产商在9月5日集中发布价格调整，聚合物与化纤原料两大板块同时出现变动。 本轮调整清单：Nayara Energy Limited于当地时间12:46宣布上调印度国内市场聚丙烯（PP）价格；HPCL-Mittal Energy Limited（HMEL）于12:43宣布上调PP价格；Indian Oil Corporation（IOCL）当日早间宣布上调精对苯二甲酸（PTA）价格、上调单乙二醇（MEG）价格，同时下调二乙二醇（DEG）价格；Reliance Industries亦于当日宣布上调PTA价格。 印度是国内定价透明度较高的聚烯烃市场之一：主要生产商采取挂牌价制度，按日或按周向国内分销体系发布价格修订，Polymerupdate等资讯平台逐条追踪。Nayara Energy运营着印度最大单一炼厂之一（Vadinar炼厂），其母公司股权由俄罗斯Rosneft牵头的财团持有；HMEL是印度国家石油公司HPCL与Mittal Energy Investments的合资企业，旗下旁遮普邦Guru Gobind Singh炼厂配有石脑油裂解和聚丙烯装置；IOCL与Reliance则是印度PTA和MEG市场的主要供应方。具体的调价幅度数据需登录Polymerupdate订阅账户查询。 从产品结构看，本轮调整呈现明显的分化特征：PP获得两大生产商一致提价，PTA获得IOCL与Reliance双线上调，MEG上行，而DEG逆势下调——同一生产链条上主产品与副产品方向相反的定价动作，通常反映各产品各自的供需松紧与库存节奏差异，而非单一成本驱动。PP-PTA-MEG-DEG链条覆盖包装、纺织化纤、薄膜等印度内需主力板块，其价格走向是观察印度制造业景气的常用高频指标，后续可关注中东局势对石脑油等上游原料成本的传导是否支撑本轮提价落地。 （来源：Polymerupdate）

headline: HPCL eyes LNG supply diversification beyond Middle East; plans Rs 5,000 crore gas investment in 3-5 years: ED Natural Gas Anuj Mehrotra
summary_text: State-run Hindustan Petroleum Corp is evaluating gas purchases from North America, Africa, and Australia to reduce its dependence on the Middle East and diversify supply base as the West Asia conflict continues to disrupt gas supplies, the company’s executive director, natural gas Anuj Mehrotra told Moneycontrol in an interview. HPCL will evaluate opportunities across the energy value chain, including potential upstream gas assets in India or overseas. ... State-run Hindustan Petroleum Corp (HPCL) is evaluating liquefied natural gas (LNG) sourcing opportunities from North America, Africa and Australia as it seeks to reduce its dependence on the Middle East and diversify its gas supply base amid continued disruptions in West Asia. The company currently sources 47 percent of its LNG from the Middle East, while Qatar is its largest supplier. HPCL Executive Director, Natural Gas Anuj Mehrotra told Moneycontrol that recent developments in the region have reinforced the need for a more diversified and flexible procurement strategy. “Going forward, diversification will be a deliberate part of our procurement strategy. We will look at sourcing opportunities from geographies such as North America, Africa, and Australia, among others, to reduce regional concentration risk. We will also continue to leverage Chhara, greenfield liquefied natural gas storage and regasification facility located in Gujarat, developed and explore additional domestic gas opportunities wherever feasible,” Mehrotra said. HPCL’s LNG portfolio combines long-term contracts with spot procurement, while the company is also exploring domestic gas opportunities. “We also see Compressed Biogas (CBG) and other renewable gases as complementary sources of energy. So, our objective is not simply to secure more LNG, but to build a resilient portfolio combining long-term LNG, spot procurement, multiple sourcing geographies, domestic gas and renewable gas,” he said. ... India imports nearly 60 percent of its total LNG from the Middle East, with Qatar accounting for 47 percent. The company’s diversification plans come as the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted gas supplies from the region. ... Around 70-80 percent of the planned investment will be directed towards city gas distribution (CGD) expansion, including strengthening steel and Medium-Density Polyethylene (MDPE) networks, adding CNG and city gas stations, expanding domestic piped natural gas (PNG) and growing industrial and commercial PNG, Mehrotra said. Around 20 percent of the investment will support LNG infrastructure, including the Chhara LNG ecosystem and LNG mobility. The remaining funds will be directed towards CBG, digitalisation, smart metering and other emerging opportunities. HPCL has already commissioned two CBG plants and plans to commission another 24 over the next five years. The company has also entered into agreements with more than 12 existing and upcoming CBG producers since 2023 for procurement of the fuel. HPCL achieved around 1.7 percent CBG blending during FY26 and is targeting 3 percent blending in FY27. “The CBG will be integrated into our CGD network and supplied through our existing infrastructure to CNG, D-PNG and Industrial & Commercial customers,” Mehrotra said. The government's CBG Blending Obligation requires CGD companies to progressively increase the share of CBG blended into CNG and PNG supplies. The blending target is 1 percent for FY26 and 3 percent for FY27. ... While the immediate focus remains on strengthening the midstream and downstream gas value chain, HPCL will also evaluate opportunities across the energy value chain, including potential upstream gas assets in India and overseas. “Any such investment would be a long-term and capital-intensive decision, and would need to be evaluated alongside our core refining, marketing and existing natural gas priorities. We would look at factors such as commercial viability, supply security, geographical diversification, strategic fit and risk-adjusted returns,” Mehrotra said. HPCL plans to commission around 45-50 new CNG stations during FY27 across its authorised geographical areas, particularly in Tier-II and Tier-III cities. It also plans to commission around five LNG dispensing stations in collaboration with other players along major highways and freight corridors. HPCL reported a consolidated net loss of Rs 12,264.67 crore in Q1FY27, compared with a net profit of Rs 4,110.93 crore in the year-ago period, as elevated crude oil prices and subdued marketing margins weighed on earnings.

headline: To augment LPG production, govt fixes facility-wise schedule to add 63,810 tonnes of cooking gas a day
summary_text: New Delhi: The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas has notified a facility-wise Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) production schedule covering public sector, joint venture and private refineries as well as upstream oil companies to maximise the production of cooking gas within the country. The schedule totals 63.81 thousand metric tonnes a day, or 63,810 tonnes a day. The order was notified on August 13 in exercise of powers under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. It amends the Petroleum Products (Maintenance of Production, Storage and Supply) Order, 1999, and came into force on the date of its publication in the Gazette. ... Chennai Petroleum Corporation Ltd's (CPCL) Manali refinery is listed at 1,480 tonnes a day. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) has two entries, Mumbai at 1,820 tonnes a day and Visakhapatnam at 2,020. Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd (MRPL) is set at 4,600 tonnes a day. Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) has three entries: Mumbai at 1,800 tonnes a day, Kochi at 4,800 and Bina at 780. At 4,800 tonnes a day, BPCL Kochi is the highest public sector entry in the Schedule. ... ## Private refiners at 25,880 tonnes a day, RIL-SEZ left blank Three private entries carry a combined 25,880 tonnes a day, or 40.6 percent of the Schedule. HPCL-Mittal Energy Ltd (HMEL) is listed at 3,400 tonnes a day. Nayara Energy is set at 4,480 tonnes a day. Reliance Industries Ltd's domestic tariff area (DTA) refinery is listed at 18,000 tonnes a day. That is the single largest entry in the schedule and accounts for 28.2 percent of the total on its own. No target has been assigned for RIL's special economic zone (SEZ) refinery. The private sector subtotal of 25,880 tonnes a day is the exact sum of the HMEL, Nayara and RIL-DTA entries, indicating that no quantity has been assigned against RIL-SEZ. Refineries in the public and private sectors together account for 57,350 tonnes a day, or 89.9 percent of the schedule. ... ## What the Order requires The new clause 3A directs all public sector, joint venture and private sector oil refining companies and upstream oil companies to develop, augment and at all times maintain adequate infrastructure for LPG storage, evacuation and transport. This may be done directly or through other entities such as railways or road tankers, and must be adequate for the quantities specified in the schedule. Companies are also directed to implement all technically and economically feasible measures and technologies to maximise LPG production beyond current minimum producible quantities as specified in the schedule. The order names naphtha-to-LPG conversion and the conversion of a gasoline-based fluid catalytic cracking unit to a petro-fluid catalytic cracking unit as examples. Any such upgrade must be intimated to the Centre for High Technology (CHT) or another authorised agency. ... ## Govt takes powers to direct a ramp-up Under sub-clause (2), the Central government may direct oil refining companies, oil marketing companies and upstream oil companies to ramp up LPG production for a specified quantity and period. It may do so if it is of the opinion that this is necessary in public interest to ensure adequate availability, equitable distribution and availability at fair prices of domestic LPG. Such directions may include compliance with restrictions on alternative uses of the input streams required to produce LPG. Companies must meet the ramp-up within the stipulated time frame. The Centre for High Technology or another authorised agency will monitor implementation. Any contravention of directions issued under the clause is punishable under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The Central government will update the Schedule on January 1 and July 1 each year. Updates will cover LPG production from new refineries and upstream companies, and additional quantities from existing facilities arising from changes to associated infrastructure, production technology, evacuation, supply, transport or distribution. ... The order follows a year in which India's LPG import exposure came under strain. India consumed 33.2 million tonnes of LPG in 2025-26, of which 13.1 million tonnes was produced domestically and the balance imported. India Ratings and Research estimated imported LPG at 64.1 percent of consumption in the fiscal. India used to source about 90 percent of its LPG imports from the Middle East, and shipping disruption in the Strait of Hormuz during the West Asia conflict hit availability. The government issued an order on March 8 directing refineries and petrochemical complexes to maximise LPG output by diverting propane, butane, propylene and butene streams to the LPG pool. Sales to industrial and commercial users were initially stopped and then scaled up gradually, the refill booking interval for households was lengthened, and households were encouraged to shift to piped natural gas. Domestic output was raised to about 55,000 tonnes a day at the peak of the crisis, and the emergency orders were withdrawn in stages after supplies eased from mid-June. ... headline: LPG Supply: Govt directs refiners to produce up to 63,810 Tons/Day till December - The HinduBusinessLine
summary_text: The Central Government has set a maximum daily production limit of 63,810 tonnes per day (TPD) of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for all the refiners in the country, including joint ventures and private sector entities, till December 2026. It is for the first time that the government has fixed a bi-annual maximum LPG production limit for refiners, which comes close on the heels of the disruption in supplies to India after closure of the Strait of Hormuz (SoH) following the latest conflict in West Asia, which began on February 28, 2026. Last week, the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas (MoPNG) through a notification, effective August 13, fixed the maximum daily LPG production limit for all the public sector, joint venture and private sector oil refining companies, and upstream oil firms. “If the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary in public interest to ensure adequate availability, equitable distribution and availability at fair prices of domestic LPG, it may by itself or through Centre for High Technology (CHT) or any other authorised agency... issue direction to oil refining companies, oil marketing companies and upstream oil companies to ramp up LPG production levels for such quantity and period specified therein, including compliance with any restrictions on alternative uses of input streams required to produce the LPG,” MoPNG said. ... The Centre will update the production schedule on January 1st and July 1st of every year including updates to LPG production from new refineries and upstream oil companies or additional LPG quantities from existing refineries and upstream companies due to changes to associated infrastructure and production technology, evacuation, supply, transport or distribution of LPG, it added. Reliance Industries (RIL) has been allocated the highest quantity of 18,000 TPD of LPG, followed by Bharat Petroleum Corporation’s (BPCL) Kochi refinery (4,800 TPD), Mangalore Refinery & Petrochemicals (4,600 TPD), Nayara Energy (4,480 TDP) and HPCL Mittal Energy (3,600 TPD). Cumulatively, all the PSU oil refining companies including Indian Oil Corporation, BPCL and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation are to produce a maximum of 31,470 TPD of LPG. While the private sector in total has been mandated to produce a maximum of 25,880 TPD of LPG, the upstream companies a maximum of 6,460 TPD. The order amends the Petroleum Products (Maintenance of Production, Storage and Supply) Order, 1999, and introduces operational directions specifically for LPG production and supply. It mandates public-sector, joint-venture and private-sector refineries, along with upstream oil companies, to develop and maintain adequate infrastructure for LPG storage, evacuation and transportation corresponding to the specified quantities. The mandate also requires the refiners to implement technically and economically viable measures to maximise LPG output beyond their existing minimum producible quantities. The technologies include naphtha-to-LPG conversion and upgrades to gasoline-based fluid catalytic cracking units into petro-fluid catalytic cracking units. “Centre for High Technology or any other authorised agency shall monitor the implementation of the directions issued under this clause. Any contravention of directions issued under this clause shall be punishable under the provisions of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955,” the notification said.

headline: India’s Russian crude imports hit record high in July - The HinduBusinessLine
summary_text: India’s crude oil imports from Russia hit a record, in value terms, at around $6.4 billion, or roughly ₹61,000 crore, last month, surpassing the June 2026 high of $5.14 billion. Analysts and refiners emphasised that Moscow has transformed into New Delhi’s strongest energy security hedge, particularly since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz (SoH) and growing disruptions in the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. The Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) pointed out that while Russia’s oil product exports hit an all-time low, India recorded its highest level of imported Russian crude ever. “India’s imports of Russian crude oil reached a record high for the second consecutive month in July 2026, rising by 2.1 per cent M-o-M and valued at euro 5.5 billion,“ it said. India’s imports of Russian crude oil reached a record high for the second consecutive month in July 2026. The increase was driven by terminals other than the two largest, Jamnagar (Reliance Industries) and Paradip (Indian Oil Corporation), it added. “Imports rose by 58 per cent at HPCL Mittal Energy (HMEL) Mundra, 35 per cent at IndianOil Vadinar SMPL and 37 per cent at Mumbai, while volumes at Jamnagar were unchanged and those at Paradip fell by 22 per cent,” CREA said. In July, Russian oil product export loadings fell 23 per cent to 4.7 million tonne (mt), their lowest level on record and less than half the 9.6 mt loaded in July 2025. Tuapse, under sustained drone attack since May, loaded almost no oil products for a second consecutive month, CREA pointed out. Overall, India was the second-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in July 2026, importing a total of Euro 6.4 billion ($7.4 billion) of Russian hydrocarbons. Crude oil constituted 87 per cent of India’s purchases, totalling Euro 5.5 billion. Coal (Euro 512 million) and oil products (Euro 341 million) constituted the remainder of their monthly Russian imports. ... In July 2026, the average price of Russia’s Urals-grade crude fell by 3 per cent month-on-month to $60.22 per barrel, still significantly higher than the EU and UK price cap of $44.1 per barrel, which took effect on February 1, 2026 and has been capped at the same level under the EU’s 21st sanctions package. The price discount of Urals-grade crude oil relative to the global benchmark Brent remained flat at 26 per cent, or $21 per barrel last month, CREA said. Despite the EU’s ban on oil products made from Russian crude, 18 shipments from refineries processing Russian crude were unloaded at EU ports in July—more than double the previous month’s total. Refineries in India, Turkiye, Brunei, and Georgia that use Russian crude exported Euro 633 million of oil products to sanctioning countries in July 2026.

headline: LPG under-recovery on cylinders narrowed to Rs 490 in July from Rs 680 in June: HPCL CMD
summary_text: New Delhi: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd's (HPCL) under-recovery on domestic LPG cylinders narrowed to Rs 490 a cylinder in July from Rs 680 in June, Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) Vikas Kaushal said on the company's Q1 FY27 earnings call on July 23, a transcript of the call released on Wednesday showed. The loss averaged Rs 510 a cylinder over the April-June quarter, according to HPCL's management. Kaushal attributed the narrowing to a fall of about USD 200 per tonne in the Saudi contract price, a key LPG marker, and to a diversification of sourcing away from the Strait of Hormuz — a market in which, he said, the industry was "once bitten twice shy." HPCL had been close to 90 percent dependent on LPG cargoes routed through Hormuz before the West Asia crisis and is now using Indian time-chartered vessels to lift cargoes from the United States (US), "which never happened in the past," he said. ... ## Rajasthan refinery ramp-up HPCL set out a ramp-up schedule for its Rajasthan refinery (HRRL), which began commercial operations in June. Its crude distillation unit is running at 60 percent capacity, and Kaushal guided to about 50 percent utilisation this quarter, 80 to 85 percent from October, and close to full utilisation on the refining section by the fourth quarter. A full run, including petrochemicals, is expected in FY28. The pet fluid catalytic cracking unit (PFCCU), which Kaushal called a "money-spinner," was hours from commissioning at the time of the call. "It's a matter of hours by which we will be able to commission it," he said. The sulphur recovery unit is the last block, expected by the end of the quarter. The refinery has begun producing motor spirit and LPG, Director (Refineries) S Bharathan said, and HPCL has stationed 150 staff from its Vizag and Mumbai refineries at the site. ... ## Cutting third-party fuel purchases Kaushal laid out a shift away from buying fuel from third parties to meet HPCL's marketing demand, a dependence he said had hit the company during the quarter. Taking diesel as an example, HPCL sourced about 50 percent from its own refineries in the first quarter, 27 percent through the HMEL joint venture and bought out 24 percent. By next year, he expects 56 percent from its own units, including the Vizag residue upgradation facility, 40 percent from joint ventures as HRRL comes on stream, and only the balance from third parties, leaving HPCL "almost self-sufficient, maybe surplus on some products." He said the change would "structurally alter our numbers" from the third quarter. ... ## HP Navya premium LPG piloted HPCL has launched HP Navya, an on-demand premium LPG product it is piloting through Swiggy in Bengaluru and its own channel in Mumbai. Kaushal said the product, launched on July 15, would be extended to 200 to 250 cities by Diwali. ... ## HRRL refinancing, JV accounting Director (Finance) Srividya Venkataraman said HPCL would refinance HRRL's high-cost rupee term loans using the RBI's fully hedged external commercial borrowing (ECB) window, worth a saving of at least 1.5 percent, and reprice bank debt now that the refinery is commissioned. At the parent level, interest cost was "not a concern," she said, with the focus on reducing the size of the debt itself. She said HRRL would be accounted for as a joint venture, reflected as a share of profit rather than consolidated. Full-year capex, guided at up to Rs 9,700 crore, is likely to come in lower as the company conserves cash, Kaushal said.

summary_text: # Smurfit Westrock Anzio: new production line inaugurated 21 October 2026 An €11 million investment at the plant near Rome expands capacity for corrugated cardboard packaging solutions and ultra-high-quality printed displays, meeting the demands of an increasingly sophisticated, growing market A new era begins for the Smurfit Westrock plant in Anzio. A state-of-the-art production line was recently inaugurated in the presence of senior management from the paper-based packaging multinational. The printing and converting line features a Koenig & Bauer Celmacch Chroma High Tech, with a 2100 × 1300 mm format and six bottom-mounted inline printing units, integrated with a Bobst Mastercut 2.1 six-colour die-cutter. This line represents state-of-the-art technology for the packaging industry, combining a working width of over two metres with exceptionally high hourly productivity, top-of-the-range quality standards and the ability to print up to six colours to the highest quality. The installation was completed according to the agreed schedule, and the line was up and running within a week, with training taking place in parallel. “This is a major investment, one of the most significant made in our country in recent years”, explains Gianluca Castellini, CEO of Smurfit Westrock Italy. “With this €11 million-plus investment, we are opening the Anzio plant up to new markets, sectors where print quality is not merely a detail but a strategic element of the brand. The Group’s decision to allocate such a substantial investment to an Italian plant is an excellent sign for our company, it complements the new corrugator, the heart of the production process, that was inaugurated at this same facility just a few years ago”. ... The benefits The new machine will increase production capacity by over 20 million square meters and boost hourly productivity by more than 20%. This capacity is expected to be fully utilized quickly, with plans already in place to pass to three-shift operations in the near future. The sustainability benefits are also significant: lower consumption despite higher performance levels; the use of high-yield water-based inks; waste optimization through precision cameras integrated into the die-cutter. These wastes, even if reduced, are reintroduced into the production process as recycled material. Indeed, Smurfit Westrock exemplifies the circular economy, where production wastes are transformed into new raw materials thanks to local recycling facilities. ... The new machine will serve clients across various sectors, including leading European food companies (particularly in the dried fruit industry) and personal care brands, that require packaging and displays with high aesthetic and functional impact in increasingly crowded markets. Specifically, the market for Shelf-Ready Packaging and coated board solutions is showing strong growth, attracting interest from food sectors such as fresh pasta and dairy, industries that had previously relied on traditional solutions and plastic materials. The new line offers a modern, sustainable, and efficient solution, equipping clients to effectively meet both competitive challenges and new European regulatory requirements. ... The new line combines high print quality, productivity, and sustainability. How important has it become for customers to find a single partner capable of combining performances, production efficiency, and compliance with new European regulatory requirements? “As packaging increasingly becomes a marketing lever and a distinguishing feature within an ever-expanding product landscape, companies are seeking partners who can combine functionality with efficiency, and sustainability with communicative effectiveness. When we add the need to comply with the new European regulations, it becomes strategic for businesses to rely on a partner who acts as a consultant rather than just a packaging manufacturer. This allows them to leverage integrated eco-design expertise and supply chain analysis tools to define the most suitable solution, while also ensuring compliance with legal obligations”.

headline: How Smurfit Westrock aims to build a more sustainable and resilient packaging future in France
summary_text: Seeking to meet the challenges of the climate crisis and regulatory changes, Smurfit Westrock is investing in its manufacturing network, accelerating decarbonization and working directly with its customers to build on its business in France. Andrew Coffey, CEO at Smurfit Westrock France, tells us more in this edition of the Spotlight. In a world that feels increasingly unpredictable the importance of strong local manufacturing has never been clearer. In our industry, the challenges of climate change and regulatory change have hastened the need to adapt. Our customers therefore need partners they can depend on more than ever, supply chains need resilience, and sustainable growth requires long-term thinking. Here in France, those priorities are shaping the decisions we make every day. That’s why we continue to invest in innovation, technology and infrastructure, ensuring we remain well positioned to support our customers and communities for years to come. ... #### Strengthening our network One of the clearest examples of that commitment is our recently announced €600 million investment programme, which will be delivered over the next three to five years. This long-term investment will strengthen our manufacturing network, modernize key facilities, accelerate decarbonization and enhance our ability to serve customers across France and Europe. Several major projects form part of this programme. These include a €40 million expansion and modernization of our Épernay facility, a further €20 million investment in our advanced corrugated plant in Vernon, and more than €100 million of investment across multiple projects at our Facture paper mill, including the installation of an evaporation plant. Together, these projects will improve efficiency, increase capacity and support our strategy for the future. ... A key part of our approach is ensuring that the facilities producing sustainable packaging are themselves operating sustainably. France is already home to four of Smurfit Westrock’s net zero plants and an almost fully decarbonized paper mill, demonstrating the significant progress we have made in reducing the environmental impact of our operations. These changes have been put in perspective by the wildfires that affected Europe this past summer – with some occurring very close to facilities in the south of France. Reducing our impact and protecting our colleagues, enabling them to work safely and effectively when challenging conditions arise, is essential to our success.

headline: Smurfit Westrock, Pratt seek investigation into ‘unfairly traded’ pizza box imports | Packaging Dive
summary_text: ### Dive Brief: - A coalition of packaging companies filed petitions this week with the U.S. Department of Commerce and the U.S. International Trade Commission requesting investigations and antidumping and countervailing duties for “unfairly traded” imports of corrugated pizza boxes from China, Malaysia and Turkey. - The group calls itself the American Pizza Boxes Manufacturers Coalition and is composed of Smurfit Westrock and Pratt Industries, according to a news release from Wiley Rein, the law firm representing the coalition. The United Steelworkers union also jointly filed the petitions. - Next, Commerce is expected to determine within 20 days whether to initiate investigations, and the USITC is expected to issue a preliminary determination within 45 days, the law firm said. The full process could take about a year, and final determinations are not likely until late 2027. ... About 3 billion pizza boxes are manufactured in the U.S. every year, Pratt Industries says. The company is considered one of the nation’s top pizza box producers and touts its 100% recycled content products. Smurfit Westrock is commonly considered the producer of the most pizza boxes in the U.S. Prior to the company’s formation via merger in 2024, legacy company WestRock had forged partnerships with foodservice giants including Domino’s and Pizza Hut on initiatives to boost pizza box recycling. ... The American Pizza Boxes Manufacturers Coalition says there has been a surge in volumes of unfairly traded pizza box imports from China, Malaysia and Turkey since 2023. These imports increased by 130% between 2023 and 2025, and have grown further in 2026 so far, the group says. These actions have caused “significant declines in production, shipments, profits, and employment” within the U.S. pizza box industry, according to Wiley Rein’s news release. The law firm declined Packaging Dive’s request to provide additional comments. The coalition says that the named countries are “dumping” pizza boxes in the United States. The USITC defines dumping as a foreign producer selling a product in the U.S. below that producer's sales price in its home market, or at a price below its cost of production. The coalition claims the boxes are being dumped in the U.S. at rates ranging from 96.62% to 568.5% from China, 110.73% from Malaysia, and 120.65% to 210.37% from Turkey. The group also alleges that the Turkish government provides “artificial advantages” via subsidies to that country’s pizza box industry. Plus, it says there’s evidence the Russian government provides cross-border subsidies that benefit producers in Turkey.

headline: Westrock Coffee’s $360m investment now a “generator of cash”, says CEO
summary_text: The US beverage manufacturer says its three-year investment programme is beginning to deliver, with new RTD and single-serve capacity supporting revenue growth, narrowing losses and a stronger pipeline of brand partners Westrock Coffee has moved into the next phase of its growth plan, reporting its fifth consecutive quarter of year-on-year improvement in adjusted EBITDA and generating positive free cash flow earlier than expected. The Arkansas-based coffee roaster, packager and supplier posted second-quarter net sales of $305.7m, up 8.8% from the same period last year. Its net loss narrowed to $13.7m from $21.6m compared to a year ago, while its operating loss fell to $1.4m from $15m. Adjusted EBITDA, Westrock’s preferred measure of underlying profitability, rose 38.9% to $21.3m. Chief Financial Officer Chris Pledger said the figures showed “continued momentum across our platform”. He added that Beverage Solutions sales rose 16.8% to $243.9m, with adjusted EBITDA up 12.7% to $22.2m. Gross profit fell 8.8% to $37.7m, however, as depreciation from the Conway assets and non-cash adjustments weighed on the quarter. ... The quarter also marked a significant milestone for a company that has spent the last three years building out its manufacturing base. Westrock invested approximately $360m in new RTD and single-serve facilities, including its 524,000-square-foot Conway, Arkansas site, which it describes as the world’s largest roast-to-RTD manufacturing facility. “The platform we spent the last three years building no longer requires capital. Rather, it is a generator of cash,” said CEO and co-founder Scott Ford. Westrock generated $20.2m in free cash flow during the quarter and was cash-flow positive for the first half of the year, one quarter ahead of its previous schedule. ... Conway is now contributing across multiple beverage channels. Ford said Beverage Solutions growth was led by higher volumes of RTD cans, glass bottles and multi-serve formats, with demand coming from both existing and new brand partners. The company is also supplying packaged coffee and single-serve cups, while expanding into adjacent categories. Pledger said growth was supported by “new customer wins in our flavours, extracts, and ingredients business, including the launch of a lemonade refreshers program”. Pledger said the company’s priorities are now to sell remaining capacity, manage its customer mix and improve operations across its plants. Ford said the business is “on the precipice of becoming a very, very different business than the one that we have been”. headline: Smurfit Westrock nearly sold out of most grades in ‘tight’ paper market | Packaging Dive
summary_text: By the numbers: Q2 2026 Net sales: $8.03B Up 1.1% year over year Net income: $88M Compared with a $26M loss in Q2 2025 Smurfit Westrock executives said during Wednesday’s earnings call that they’re overall pleased with second-quarter performance and anticipate a stronger second half of the year. North American corrugated volumes were down 4.5% year over year, which was “in line with our expectations as we continue to execute on our value-over-volume strategy,” said CFO Ken Bowles. Company executives and analysts all noted that the containerboard market is strengthening and has tightened significantly in roughly a six-week period this summer. “People did not expect for the market to change so rapidly,” said CEO Tony Smurfit. “Nobody would have been pre-buying.” Barring Smurfit Westrock’s limited sales of coated recycled paperboard, the company is essentially sold out for all paper grades and is in “catch-up mode” for the remainder of the year, he said. “Global paper markets today are as strong as I have seen in my lifetime within this industry,” Smurfit said, adding that conditions for nearly all grades are “as tight as I can remember.” ... Much of the call centered on Smurfit Westrock’s and the broader industry’s recent rounds of fiber price increases. On Tuesday, analysts reported that SW announced a $100 per ton increase for both containerboard and kraft paper set to take effect Sept. 1. That followed Packaging Corporation of America’s July 24 announcement of a $140 per ton increase, which many have called unprecedented, kicking off this year’s third round of containerboard industry price hikes that has also included International Paper, among others. Earlier in July, SW announced a 4% to 6% increase on SBS folding carton, commercial print and foodservice grades as of Aug. 10 — its second SBS increase this year. SW executives repeatedly mentioned that these increases are necessary due to rising input costs, especially energy and freight, which have skyrocketed largely because of the war with Iran. SW now expects annual North American and European input costs to be $300 million more than anticipated three months ago, Smurfit said. The rising cost of freight “remains the most significant headwind we face in 2026,” Bowles said. “That inflationary cost environment is not showing signs of abatement, and we will continue to evaluate all options available to us as we progress through the remainder of this year.” ... ### Closing more facilities Executives discussed a recent mill closure in the U.K. and noted “a number of closures” had occurred in North America, EMEA and APAC. SW also disclosed it’s in the process of closing eight additional converting facilities in both Europe and North America. Smurfit discussed improvements to existing assets and characterized the remaining “number of lossmakers that we have” as “probably around 20.” That’s down from close to 80 so-called lossmakers when the company formed two years ago after Smurfit Kappa acquired WestRock. “We’ve got some great box plants, and we've got some not-so-great box plants. Those not-so-great box plants need to improve,” Smurfit said. ... SW delisted from the London Stock Exchange on June 22 and will remain solely on the New York Stock Exchange. Smurfit said the company is already seeing self-improvement in alignment with the medium-term plan introduced in February. There’s a “strong pipeline of new corrugated business moving through August and into September” that should help boost performance in the second half of the year, Bowles said. Executives expressed optimism about further volume growth in H2. The company now projects adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization for the year to total $4.9 billion to $5.1 billion, down from earlier projections of $5 billion to $5.3 billion. Executives expect $2.4 billion to $2.5 billion in capital expenditures this year.

headline: International Paper entertains offers for EMEA business | Packaging Dive
summary_text: IP confirmed it has received unsolicited offers for the independent company it’s spinning off in the Europe, Middle East and Africa region. ... International Paper has received unsolicited bids for the company it plans to spin off, the fiber producer confirmed in a statement Thursday afternoon. The company also noted it was aware of “recent movement in the share price” following the Financial Times first reporting Thursday that private equity firms Lone Star and Atlas Holdings were pursuing deals to purchase the spinoff company. FT also reported that other PE firms had been in the mix, but only the named two remain. IP’s stock price rose more than 7% Thursday following the report. The Memphis,Tennessee-based company announced on Jan. 29 — almost exactly one year after acquiring London-based DS Smith — that it was going to split into two companies based on geography: one in North America and one in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. IP has repeatedly projected that the split would be finalized early in 2027. Up until now, IP had not suggested it would sell that spinoff company. But it confirmed in Thursday’s statement that it’s “progressing the Spin Off and evaluating the Potential Sale in parallel.” IP said the discussions about an EMEA business sale are at an early stage and it cannot guarantee that such a deal will occur. It also said it couldn’t assure what “the ultimate timing or structure of the proposed separation of the EMEA Packaging Business from International Paper” would look like. International Paper announced Wednesday it will hold a Capital Markets Day on Nov. 3, during which it plans to discuss progress related to separating the EMEA business into an independent, publicly traded company. headline: Two firms are reportedly considering bids for International Paper's (IP) European unit, FT reports citing sources | Newsquawk
summary_text: Two firms are reportedly considering bids for International Paper's (IP) European unit, FT reports citing sources. ## What it means A two-bidder report on a carved-out regional unit is the classic shape of a process already underway rather than unsolicited interest, and with only two names in the frame the competitive tension is thin: outcomes in such processes have historically hinged on whether the seller can credibly threaten to retain the asset or run a dual-track, since a limited buyer set tends to compress the premium. The relevant distinction is strategic versus financial sponsorship: strategic buyers in packaging have typically been able to underwrite higher multiples through synergies and consolidation logic, while sponsor interest has been more sensitive to financing conditions and the unit's standalone cash conversion. Carve-outs of this kind also carry execution risk around entanglements, shared sites, and transitional services, which is where comparable deals have tended to slip timetable or reprice. What is worth watching is confirmation of the bidders' identities and whether a process adviser or deadline surfaces, both of which have historically signalled how far along the sale genuinely is. As a sourced report rather than a confirmed process, the gap between report and formal announcement has in past episodes been where these stories most often stall or widen to additional parties.

headline: 3 paper packaging CEOs talk market volatility, pricing | Packaging Dive
summary_text: Economic and geopolitical disruptions are heavily impacting paper and packaging businesses and creating market volatility, according to fiber company executives who spoke at the Jefferies Global Industrials Conference on Thursday. Cost inflation universally continues to pose a drag. OCC prices have gone up notably, presenting a “$400 million, $500 million swing in this year alone,” according to International Paper CEO Andy Silvernail. Fuel and transport costs also are significantly higher due to the war with Iran. “We all know those challenges that are out there, and they’re undeniable,” Silvernail said of trade, tariffs and conflict. “At the same time, what it does is it sets the context for how you can compete.” Price increases are one of the ways these companies are trying to recoup costs. Producers have announced three rounds of containerboard price hikes this year, with the most recent particularly coming under fire for the hefty price tags — $140 per ton for Packaging Corporation of America and $80 per ton for IP. ... ### IP adapts to demand squeeze Silvernail reiterated claims that supply is tight. Yet demand, while steady, also is lagging expectations, in part because consumers have been hard hit by inflation the last couple years. “In our estimation, over 2.5 years it’s cost about five points of aggregate demand,” Silvernail said. “In the broad scale of the K-shaped economy that we all talk about, that bottom of that K is being squeezed.” All conditions considered, demand likely will remain muted for the remainder of this year and throughout 2027, he said. In addition, fruit and vegetable recalls stemming from cyclosporiasis outbreaks are affecting produce customers on the West Coast, creating a short-term negative impact to IP’s demand. These dynamics have pushed IP to be more aggressive with removing costs and relying on price increases. Pricing is expected to be a “major tailwind” in 2027 as the most recent hikes are recognized. IP cut about 15% of box capacity from its production network in the last two years, and reinvestments are underway. “We've been reinvesting very aggressively back into our mill and our converting systems to drive productivity, and we're certainly seeing the gains,” Silvernail said. He referenced the company restructuring underway in Europe and ongoing efforts to close more than 40 facilities there and cut 4,000 employees. While these moves are “aggressive,” they’re “necessary,” Silvernail said. Overall for the company, “the noise that has been around the business in terms of restructuring, in terms of asset sales, that will come to a close where we'll start really driving the business on a normalized basis.”

headline: International Paper at Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026: focus tightens By Investing.com
summary_text: International Paper Company (IP) used Thursday, 10 September 2026, at the Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 to outline a business that is being reshaped around North American packaging, even as demand stays soft and costs remain volatile. Chief Executive Andy Silvernail said the company is leaning on restructuring, asset sales and new investment to improve its cost position and customer service while preparing for a separation of its European operations. Silvernail said the macro backdrop remains difficult, with trade tariffs, energy inflation and weak consumer spending weighing on the industry. Still, he argued that the company is focusing on what it can control, from plant closures and commercial discipline to reliability and product quality. “Whatever given period of time when the macro gets distorted for whatever reason,” he said, “you grab onto those things that you can absolutely control.” ... ## Key takeaways - International Paper is moving from a diversified paper and packaging model toward a more focused North American packaging business. - Management said about $700 million of EBITDA improvement in North America over two years came entirely from cost cuts. - The company expects demand to remain muted through 2027, with North America flat for the rest of 2026 and Europe softer. - Capital spending is still elevated at 9% to 9.5% of sales, but is expected to settle around 7.5% over time. - Pricing actions, tighter supply and a leaner asset base are expected to support margins into 2027. ... ## Financial results and cost pressures Silvernail said International Paper has delivered about $700 million of EBITDA improvement in North America over the past two years. He said the gain came from cost reduction, with inflation and pricing largely offsetting each other. - North America EBITDA improved by about $700 million over two years. - Inflation and pricing have effectively balanced out over that period. - Announced pricing is expected to have an incremental profit benefit in 2027. - Management described pricing as a major tailwind for next year. The company also laid out several cost exposures that could affect results. Despite these headwinds, shares have declined 21.77% over the past year to trade at $34.64, though InvestingPro analysis suggests the stock is undervalued at current levels. The company maintains a dividend yield of 5.34% and has paid dividends for 56 consecutive years. While International Paper was not profitable over the last twelve months, analysts expect the company to return to profitability this year, with earnings per share forecast at $1.33 for fiscal 2026. - Diesel sensitivity is about $95 million for each $1.00 per gallon on an annualized basis. - Diesel prices have risen about $2.00 per gallon in the last six months, creating a $150 million to $200 million headwind. - Old corrugated cardboard, or OCC, could swing 2026 results by about $400 million to $500 million. - For 2027, total inflation exposure could vary by about $400 million on either side of the midpoint, depending on the mix of inflation assumptions. ... International Paper said it produces 70% of its own energy in the U.S., leaving the rest of its exposure mainly tied to natural gas and diesel. In Europe, the company faces higher energy volatility, especially from natural gas. Capital spending remains heavy because of a broad modernization program. Capex is currently running at about 9% to 9.5% of sales and is expected to normalize to about 7.5% of sales over time. Management said the company is investing across 80 facilities and moving capital away from high-cost, low-return assets toward lower-cost, higher-return operations. ... ## Operational updates and restructuring International Paper has spent the past two years reshaping its footprint, especially in Europe. Silvernail described the restructuring as aggressive but necessary. - About 40 facilities in Europe have been closed since the program began. - About 4,000 employees have exited as part of the restructuring. - The company also announced the closure of a paper machine at Kemsley in the U.K. - Management said the European program is on track for completion within the previously stated 12 to 15 month window. He said the company has moved from being “very long” in paper capacity 2.5 years ago to being “modestly short” now, after shutting higher-cost capacity. That shift, he said, has helped create a tighter market and better discipline across the business. ... In North America, the company has also changed how it sells and serves customers. Silvernail said the sales force has grown by about 40%, while compensation has been shifted from a heavily guaranteed model to one that is more incentive-based. The company has also adopted more data-driven commercial tools, including artificial intelligence analytics, pricing discipline, pipelining, market segmentation and an 80/20 approach. He said customer satisfaction in North America has improved as the company has invested in reliability, quality, service and innovation. Recent investments include: - A new converter in Phoenix, which management said is improving productivity and responsiveness. - Riverdale, which is ramping “very nicely.” - Mansfield, which is showing “really substantial gains.” - Norpak, which management said could deliver very high returns for relatively low capital. - The Dover box plant acquisition, part of the broader asset shift. - With a market capitalization of $18.34 billion and revenue of $24.2 billion over the last twelve months, International Paper remains a prominent player in the Containers & Packaging industry, according to InvestingPro analysis. ... International Paper said about 14% to 15% of its box assets have been removed from the system. It expects further consolidation as productivity gains allow it to optimize the network. Management said the “easy stuff” has mostly been done, and future changes will depend more on continued productivity improvements. ... Silvernail said the North American market remains tight, and he expects it to stay that way. Among other things, we see positive effects from the acquisition of Seti, completed at the end of 2024. Together with Duni's organization in Italy, we have strengthened our presence in Southern Europe and created new opportunities for profitable growth in the region. The development during the year confirms the value of building a more balanced geographical presence in Europe and reducing dependence on individual markets. Within Dining Solutions, we are now launching our lighting platform d.ls, broadening our offering to the hotel and restaurant market. At the same time, we continue to develop Food Packaging Solutions through Duniform, where the combination of machines, service and packaging solutions creates an increasingly strong offering for customers in the food industry. In parallel with our growth initiatives, we are also implementing the cost savings program communicated in the previous quarter. **What are the most important priorities during the final months of the year?** The main priority is to complete the logistics transition in a controlled manner while continuing to improve quality and efficiency throughout the business, with particular focus on transportation costs. In parallel, we are working to create conditions for continued growth by strengthening our customer offering, developing our market positions and ensuring that we are well positioned as activity among our customers gradually increases. **What gives you the greatest confidence ahead of 2027?** Through the changes and investments we are making in production, logistics and our product portfolio, we create better conditions for the future. During the year, we have also adapted to the prevailing market conditions through cost-saving programs within sales and administration. As a result, we will enter 2027 with a stronger operational platform than we had at the beginning of the year.
