The game will be produced using the FMV method, which utilizes actual actors' performances and filmed footage within the game. Its distinctive feature lies in combining the narrative immersion of movies and dramas with the interactivity of games. ... 'Story Island' plans to expand its capabilities accumulated during video content production—casting, filming, directing, and storytelling—to the new platform of games, thereby broadening the scope of utilization for its content IP.

headline: Passion Distribution Announces Third International Adaptation of Virgin Island - TTV News
summary_text: Passion Distribution has announced the third international adaptation of Virgin Island in 2026. The social experiment format, originally produced by Double Act for Channel 4, has been commissioned by TV 2 Denmark, with Banijay Entertainment label Nordisk Film TV producing the local version. The Danish adaptation, which has recently wrapped filming in Greece, will follow a group of young men and women as they confront issues surrounding intimacy and relationships. The deal follows adaptations commissioned by Dutch public broadcaster BNNVARA, produced by Concept Street, and RTL+ in Germany, produced by RTL Studios. Passion Distribution also confirmed that several additional international versions are currently in development. ... Virgin Island became Channel 4’s biggest streaming launch in its history across any genre. Its first season also delivered the broadcaster’s highest consolidated share among 16–34-year-olds since modern records began, performing at four times the channel’s benchmark for the demographic. The second season, which premiered in 2026, further strengthened the format’s performance. In May, it grew its 16–34 audience by 11% year on year and became the most-watched programme of the month among this demographic across all UK commercial channels, outperforming titles including Gogglebox, The Great Pottery Throw Down and Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins.

headline: Chinese Short Drama Platforms Expand Influence in South Korea | Aju Press
summary_text: Chinese short-form drama platforms operating in South Korea are rapidly expanding their influence while remaining outside the telecommunications provider registration and management system. These platforms, which offer content with high levels of suggestiveness and violence, are in a regulatory gray area, leaving the government unable to track their domestic revenue or user numbers. According to Lee Joo-hee, a lawmaker from the Democratic Party, an investigation into 11 Chinese short drama platforms, including DramaBox, LilShot, and TopShot, revealed that none had registered as telecommunications providers. However, this is not considered a violation of current laws. Foreign firms providing services from abroad without a domestic entity are classified as 'cross-border service providers' and are exempt from registration requirements under the World Trade Organization's General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS) and free trade agreements (FTAs). ... While platforms like Netflix and Disney+ have registered local entities and are subject to regulatory oversight, Chinese short drama platforms operate directly through apps without a domestic presence, leading to differing regulatory treatment among foreign video platforms. ... The concern lies in the content offered by these unregistered platforms. With inconsistent review standards and the ability to access 15+ rated content without logging in, there are growing worries, but the government lacks effective means to manage and supervise these services. ... Under the Telecommunications Business Act, the obligation to designate a domestic agent applies only to providers with an average daily user count exceeding 1 million in the previous year or a domestic traffic share of over 1%. Since the scale of these platforms is unclear, it is uncertain whether they meet this criterion. Lee added, "Even if the government requests data submission or seeks to address user harm, the lack of administrative contact domestically may hinder enforcement efforts." ... Amid this regulatory gap, Chinese short dramas are seeing a sharp increase in both viewing time and user numbers. According to Mobile Index, the average monthly usage time for ShortMax in June was 332 minutes, which is 88% of the time spent on Tving (376 minutes) and 72% of that on Wavve (464 minutes). DramaBox (260 minutes) and LilShot (201 minutes) also significantly outperformed Coupang Play (71 minutes). ... The average usage time for the three platforms—DramaBox, LilShot, and ShortMax—rose from 248 minutes in January to 264 minutes in June, while the average for domestic OTT platforms Tving, Wavve, and Coupang Play decreased from 328 minutes to 304 minutes, narrowing the gap from 80 minutes to nearly 40 minutes. Monthly active users (MAU) for LilShot surged from 64,529 in January to 389,160 in July, nearly a sixfold increase (503%), while DramaBox approached 1 million users with 919,761.

headline: Under Salt Marsh indie reveals expansion plans - The Knowledge Online
summary_text: ## Little Door Productions brings in Pulse and See-Saw creatives ... Under Salt Marsh outfit Little Door Productions has bolstered its creative team as part of its expansion plans beyond its Wales heartland, according to chief executive Elwen Rowlands. Joining the company are Abigail Dennis and Emily Precious as development producer and head of production, respectively. ... Dennis was ... senior development producer at ... Films ... -led ... development ... designed ... managed the ... ’ ... new ... initiative ... . ... , ... Film ... . ... ### Beyond Wales ... Rowlands has set bold growth ambitions for Little Door, underpinned by the recently opening of a London office to complement its Cardiff headquarters. Rowlands says the move is about practicality, noting the importance of having a physical presence near where most key industry gatekeepers are based. The indie, which also produced BBC1 drama The Pact, was founded in 2020 by Rowlands and Little Door’s chief operating officer Hayley Manning, who is based in Newcastle. Rowlands splits her week between Cardiff and London, with staff deployed between the two locations. “The day-to-day of our industry happens in London: commissioners, agents, distributors, international partners [are there]. It’s vital to have a foothold here, so that we can build those relationships,” she explained. ... Indeed, Little Door is in pre-production on its first project set outside Wales, though details are heavily under-wraps. ... The success of Sky original crime thriller Under Salt Marsh has also helped dispel presumptions around Little Door’s capabilities. Rowlands acknowledged that it is a Welsh story, based in Wales, but it was not a cheap show. The climate change-infused murder mystery notched up 1.8m viewer in its first week of release, becoming Sky’s biggest original drama since The Day of the Jackal launched in 2024. ... With the arrival of Dennis and Precious, a new project going into production, and still riding the wave of Under Salt Marsh’s success, Rowlands admitted it’s a “good moment” for Little Door. “We need to capitalise on it, so it makes sense to bring in a team that can help us build the slate and get everything market ready as soon as possible.”

headline: LC Waikiki Partnership Secured for Dav Pilkey’s Dog Man
summary_text: Dog Man is set for a major international retail expansion as Fauna Entertainment announces a multi-territory licensing partnership with LC Waikiki, spanning more than 60 countries and over 1,300 stores worldwide. The partnership was brokered through local Turkey agent, Fauna, and worldwide agent The Joester Loria Group on behalf of Dav Pilkey’s Monster Island for the Dog Man and Cat Kid Comic Club properties. The first wave of Dog Man products has begun arriving in stores, featuring a broad lifestyle and apparel assortment that includes children’s apparel, sleepwear, socks and water bottles. Leveraging LC Waikiki’s extensive retail footprint across Europe, MENA and beyond, the launch brings Dog Man to millions of consumers. Fauna Entertainment is building on this momentum to expand the brand’s international presence, with additional licensing opportunities already underway across multiple categories.

headline: ITV Results: Studios Bosses Confident Despite America Revenue Dip
summary_text: ITV Studios bosses are remaining bullish in the face of declining U.S. and international revenues as the Love Island maker prepares to be unleashed onto the market. Of concern for ITV Studios, this morning’s ITV half-year results showed a 17% revenue decline in the U.S. and a 24% slide internationally, reflecting a reversal of previous fortunes. On a results call with press, ITV Studios chief Julian Bellamy put this mainly down to a “softening of demand” in the free-to-air space and said it “underlines the broader importance” of the producer-distributor pushing further into making shows for streamers and developing its Zoo 55 digital arm. “Let’s not forget, we’re on the up,” Bellamy said bullishly, as he pointed out that overall ITV Studios revenues grew 2% during the first six months of this year to £912M ($1.2B). “We feel confident about the progress we are making.” ... ITV Studios has made growth with the American streamers a cornerstone of its strategy over the past few years and there will nevertheless be jitters about the decline in revenue across the pond. Helping allay those jitters are some big shows set to deliver during the latter half of 2026 including The Gentlemen Season 2 for Netflix and Apple TV’s Guilty Creatures, both made by ITV Studios indies. When the Sky-ITV deal completes around this time next year, ITV Studios will be unleashed onto the market and will become a publicly listed company. ... McCall backed ITV Studios today as having “terrific competitive advantages” with “extraordinary IP” and refused to budge on the question of whether ITV Studios will look for a buyer once it becomes independent. This came a few days after the CEO of Banijay downplayed the idea of the French behemoth swooping for ITV Studios now that it is merging with All3Media.

headline: The Government is boosting the global children's animation franchise 'Milo' with a multi-million dollar investment
summary_text: The Spanish government, through the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT), has announced a public investment of €9,2 million in the children's animated audiovisual project 'Milo'. This operation, which mobilizes a total of €18,8 million, is part of a public-private partnership involving two Spanish companies: Planeta Junior, based in Catalonia, and Amuse Animation, based in the Canary Islands. The goal is to transform the preschool series into a global entertainment franchise. ... 'Milo' was created in 2021 for the British children's channel Milkshake! and has since become a global phenomenon. It airs in over 170 countries, is dubbed into more than 20 languages , and is available on over 45 channels and platforms. In Spain, it premiered on Clan (RTVE) in May 2022, and in the fall of 2024, it arrived on the American public television network PBS Kids, becoming the first European preschool series in over a decade to achieve this. Its third season is currently in production and is scheduled to premiere in 2027. ... SETT, attached to the Ministry for Digital Transformation and Public Administration, is contributing €9,2 million, while the remaining funding comes from private collaboration. The new company will be dedicated to exploiting the rights to 'Milo' in multiple formats and territories, beyond just audiovisual content. According to government sources, the entire content production will take place in Spain, which boosts the national industrial base, generates skilled employment, and strengthens the sector's value chain. ... Planeta Junior, part of DeAPlaneta Entertainment (a joint venture between Grupo Planeta and DeAgostini), acquired full ownership of the brand in 2025. Amuse Animation, led by Rubén Zarauza and Elena Catalán, will participate in the production of the new episodes, expanding the franchise's creative and production capabilities. This operation falls within the second phase of the Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan , funded by the European Union through the Next Generation EU funds, and is part of the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan. ... The project extends beyond the television series. The 'Milo' roadmap includes the development of apps, video games, licensing agreements, and consumer products, as well as live experiences. The brand will feature a global toy line developed by Rainbow Designs , and expansion into gaming and interactive experiences is planned. Ignacio Segura de Lassaleta, CEO of DeAPlaneta Entertainment, stated that SETT's investment confirms the strength and international potential of 'Milo,' allowing them to solidify a long-term, sustainable growth strategy.

headline: Little Lion’s flagship immersive gaming experience to open September 5
summary_text: Little Lion Entertainment is set to launch its new immersive gaming destination on September 5, which it says marks a significant milestone in the company's continued expansion of the live video game attraction sector. Located in London, UK, Arcade Arena London will bring together three large-scale immersive gaming experiences under one roof, which the brand described as its most ambitious investment to date. ... The new entertainment centre launches with three immersive attractions. The Pac-Man Live Experience, developed in partnership with Bandai Namco Entertainment, turns the recognisable video game franchise into a fully immersive live attraction. Also featured within Arcade Arena London is Chaos Karts, Little Lion Entertainment's original immersive karting concept. The go-karting experience combines electric karts with digitally projected gaming worlds to create an interactive racing experience. Finally, Alien Invasion, a brand-new experience, will make its debut in the immersive gaming experience. It will combine immersive storytelling, advanced digital and drone technology and live-action gameplay within a science fiction environment.

headline: Little Island, Big Ideas: How New York’s Most Unusual Outdoor Venue Crafts Its Lineup | Show News
summary_text: # Little Island, Big Ideas: How New York’s Most Unusual Outdoor Venue Crafts Its Lineup Published July 28, 2026 at 5:55 pm Author Daniel Ortiz Some artistic directors determine the seasonal programming for a theater, opera house or community space. Zack Winokur, however, has an island unto himself. For the last three seasons, Winokur has served as the producing artistic director of Little Island, the artificial island/public park adjacent to Manhattan’s Meatpacking District in the Hudson River which opened five years ago. While the Juilliard-educated Winokur had directed, produced and/or cocreated theatrical and opera productions prior to this gig (he also co-founded the imaginative American Modern Opera Company in 2017 and serves as its artistic director), Little Island at Pier 55 is unlike any other performance space in a city that has no shortage of them. Not only is it outdoors, but, as the name suggests, it’s a literal island. Unlike, say, theatrical performances in Central Park, Little Island presents artists and innovators with the opportunity to shape the audio-visual experience of an entire discrete outdoor space. ... This season, Little Island features new works from returning musical iconoclasts (Justin Vivian Bond opens the season with Summer’s Eve from July 29-31; Anthony Roth Costanzo takes a tour through minimalist music history from Aug. 5-9; Laurie Anderson participates in Thomas Bartlett’s Allen Ginsberg at 100 from Sept. 2-6) as well as excavations of New York City’s rich musical foundations (The Late Show with Stephen Colbert bandleader Louis Cato brings the music of the Savoy and Harlem Renaissance back to raucous life from Aug. 19-23; three-time Grammy winner Cécile McLorin Salvant explores the edges of Tin Pan Alley from Aug. 12-16). Additionally, creative trailblazers are bringing their distinct visions to the island. Tony winner Qween Jean throws a Summer Legacy Ball extravaganza on Aug. 1, and from Aug. 27-30, Julio Torres and Martine Gutierrez premiere Marina, “an underwater fairytale about love, belonging and catfishing” (what else would you expect from the boundary-free brain of Torres?) commissioned by the 2026 Whitney Biennial. Throughout the entire season, Papi Juice parties — thrown by the Brooklyn DJ/art collective centered around uplifting queer and trans people of color — will bring free dance parties to the island’s “Play Ground.” The Papi Juice parties always dovetail with one of the performances at The Amph, Little Island’s 700-plus-seat amphitheater – meaning you can catch a show, grab a drink and shake your thing all on the same night on the same island. ... Ahead of Little Island’s 2026 season, Billboard spoke with Winokur about how he approaches programming the bespoke space, what we can expect from this year’s slate and why certain Little Island performances remind him of MTV Unplugged or “the parade of animals going to the Big Apple Circus.” ... this role ... It actually is a weird, circuitous route. Before the park was built, I was starting my own company, the American Modern Opera Company, AMOC, and we were in conversations to do a show well before the park was built. That never happened. And then when it opened in the first summer, Mikki Shepard ran this really beautiful free festival that was super dense — I think it was just one month, but just gigantic. And my company did a show of all Julius Eastman’s music that was the closing night of the opening festival. Then Barry Diller [billionaire businessperson who commissioned Little Island] called me and asked me to think about a new approach to programming, and we came up with this thought of doing more original programming. I started my first season in 2024. ... you ... talking to ... Was there ... the kind of ... you were ... ? ... I think the thing that we were most excited about, and certainly I was most excited about, was a couple of things. One is that we so rarely think of performance as part of public art, and the idea of doing shows in a public park feels incredibly special. So one of the points was to bring a real high-low sensibility to a public space and to make it as accessible as possible, which is why so much of our programming is free and the maximum ticket price is $25. And I was always really interested in extraordinary people, and people particularly who live here or are inflected by the city in one way or another. I think so many of the things that we’re doing this year, and that we’ve reflected on in the past, are about different scenes or icons from the past, the present and the future, all colliding in one place on the island. If that makes sense. ... It does. In terms of audience, who is Little Island programming for? I think it reflects who visits the park, actually, which is always a very interesting thing. In the summers we have days that are 13,000 people just visiting the park without performances happening. What’s interesting about it is that it has quickly become an iconic place in the city, and therefore it’s a very popular destination for tourists. But it’s also a neighborhood park. You see the same people running through it, the same families coming through every morning. That was the thing I’m thinking about all the time in terms of the programming as well — that it should be attractive to anybody, and it should feel like a space that is extremely for New Yorkers without being exclusive at all. ... It’s a mixture of things. I’m always on the lookout for people who surprise me. I’m also always interested in asking people who I just think are extraordinary to do something a little bit further to the edge of what they normally do — and also putting back into the center things that are on the edges. So I think about this sense of the neighborhood and its icons — thinking about past seasons with the likes of Twyla Tharp and Qween Jean, who’s returning, and Charles Ludlam and Justin Vivian Bond, who is a scene all to herself, and even Meshell Ndegeocello taking on Baldwin [in 2025]. These are all people exploring moments that defined New York, and that also might define the future of our city. Even things like this season — we have Florent coming to the island, who had this extremely famous diner in the Meatpacking District [from 1985-2008]. So also things that are also hyper, hyper local. ... Really, though. Climate change is doing its thing, and the last few years in New York have been really been brutal with these heat waves. How challenging is that for programming? Yeah, it’s just affected life. It’s really tough. We do our best to just put on the show, no matter what. There are certain things that we just can’t do because it’s unsafe — with lightning or whatever. But thankfully, we’re at night, so by evening it usually is a tolerable heat. And one of the things I feel like people don’t always know is that, in addition to delicious lemonade and water, there are also cocktails available and a liquor license across the entire island, so you can always be drinking, which I think helps mediate any weather issues at all. It’s just one of those things that I think is so special about this venue. It certainly makes it difficult that it’s uncovered and outdoors. However, when it is a gorgeous night, which it often is, there is simply nothing better than being able to have a cocktail, watch an unbelievable show, look at the Hudson River under the stars, and then to walk out on any of these Friday nights in our season and stumble into a Papi Juice party. That’s a thing that can only happen on Little Island and only happen in New York. ... Well, one of the things I’ve always loved about this space is that it’s a thrust stage, so it’s actually really intimate, even though it’s over 700 seats. You’re never that far away from any performer, and that intimacy is something we’ve always tried to find the happy medium of. Figaro is a great example of something that felt really grand, like a great spectacle, but also homespun and very nuanced. To have an orchestra that’s only eight players playing that music, and the sound system is so extraordinary that you really feel like — in a weird way — this is what opera was meant to be. Or how opera was meant to be experienced, rather than in a gigantic space. ... Then I ... about these other moments — Jeremy Denk and Conor Hanick playing Ives, or Meshell Ndegeocello — moments that harken back for me to an MTV Unplugged moment, where just these unbelievable superstar people are so close, and also not on a proscenium, just out in the ... of this island. That feeling is where it feels most like a neighborhood park — like this is a public living room, and that is incredibly special. ... I’ve also always loved the fact that it’s wonderful that every show has always been sold out, and that even when things are packed and the standing rail is packed, if you are a tourist or a local who’s just walking in the neighborhood and didn’t expect to see a show, you still can get one. We’ve linked all of the speaker systems throughout the park so that the music happening in The Glade or in The Amph can be heard in the Play Ground. You have these beautiful vantage points from all of the pathways, so if you don’t have a ticket, you can still see and experience the show in a really fabulous way. I don’t think there is another theater that just doesn’t have walls. What that symbol means in the city, to me, is one of the greatest gifts that’s ever happened. ... In terms of the actual Amph space, before a show opens, how many times do they get to run through it? It totally depends on what it needs. It’s always a little bit of a game of Tetris, because the season is only so long and there are only so many shows, and we want to have as many public performances as possible. In the past, it’s always been really interesting to me. I remember my first season we opened with this new Twyla Tharp piece, and there were weeks of tech rehearsal — and of course the tech rehearsal is happening in the theater in the public park. So tech rehearsal was watched every single night. I couldn’t believe it. ... We ... people the ... they need. ... person who does this ... that ... ’ ... enough time for anything, ... we ... people the time that they need ... what the project is. And thankfully the sound ... is surprisingly wonderful, so it’s usually pretty quick to get it sounding great. ... I’m a very hands-on producer. Particularly on past commissions, like Figaro or Twyla, it’s incredibly involved and hands-on. I think that good creative producing is being a collaborator, not just being an investor. On many of the projects we have this season that are more concert based, it’s just an incredibly delicious tossing around of ideas — being a sounding board and a thought partner to everybody. ... It’s definitely not a nine-to-five. We’re in this delicious moment right now where everything’s loaded in, so all of the lights are up and all of the speakers on the catenary system are there, which takes a while to get up. A normal day is moving between meetings with these artists to check how things are going, to be in conversation with them, looking at the order of these concerts, making sure that stage layouts are making sense, making sure that everybody’s backline is in order. Today I did a couple of site visits with designers and lighting designers, to step onto the stage and make sure we’ve walked through it, looking at what’s possible. I have an unbelievable, incredibly dedicated team. Once we go into production, it’s this wild thing where we are in the office and then we are at all of the shows, making sure that everything is good. ... I’m there basically every single night, and it’s one of the treats. If I’m being totally honest, I’ve basically lived here since I was 15, and I had never spent a summer in New York until I got this job — like a full summer. To be able to be on the island with all of the visitors, and have a drink, have a snack, and then take in a free show in the Glade, and then a beautiful show in the amphitheater, and then one of these Papi Juice parties — it’s amazing. It’s just a totally amazing place. ... And there’s quite a variety. It’s not a Broadway theater where they have the same show for months, years even. Every few nights you’re switching to something else. ... Part of the fun has always been that it’s a season. The fun of making a season is figuring out how things both complement each other and collide with one another and balance each other. One of the things I love is that, especially on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, there are at least two shows a night in the different spaces. ... And back to an earlier question about what I’m learning about the space — one of the things that feels really amazing that we learned, I think with Arthur Russell first, was that we could do six hours of uninterrupted music, and we could also transform how people entered the space. There was this whole drone improvisation with Sam Amidon and Laurie Anderson walking around with their instruments throughout the entire park. Those moments where the whole 2.4-acre park becomes one big idea and one canvas is something we’re exploring more this year and is something you can’t do anywhere else. It would be like a Broadway show getting to control the entire street they’re on. The drinks, the food, what you’re hearing when you step across the highway onto that bridge — being able to design that entire experience is very special.

summary_text: Skydance has pledged to keep CNN and CBS News editorially independent. But with roughly $80 billion in debt hanging over the combined company, keeping the two newsrooms separate may be easier than keeping their operations that way. The company is targeting at least $6 billion in merger cost reductions from its $110 billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, while insisting most of the cuts won’t come from jobs. Combining office space, technology and production facilities could yield savings without affecting editorial decisions. Sharing bureaus, crews and other newsgathering resources would be more complicated. ... Skydance’s own executives have left room for questions about where the company will draw that line. Asked on CNBC last week whether CNN and CBS News could consolidate newsgathering to reduce costs, co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said, “This isn’t about cost savings in this case,” describing the networks as “two separate businesses.” Co-CEO David Ellison, meanwhile, acknowledged there are “absolutely operational efficiencies” to be found. ... Those mixed messages leave open a range of potential cuts. Interviews with current and former media executives suggest Skydance could find relatively straightforward savings in facilities, technology and production, while larger opportunities may lie in international newsgathering. But consolidating bureaus, crews and other reporting resources could force decisions about which journalists cover which stories, potentially testing the company’s promise to keep CNN and CBS News editorially independent. ... The question now is whether common ownership can create meaningful efficiencies without making the two news operations function as one. “Simply living under the same roof does not guarantee anything,” Jon Klein, the former president of CNN/U.S. who previously worked at CBS News, told TheWrap. Klein said common ownership creates opportunities behind the scenes, but does not automatically make two news operations work better together. He added that there are production efficiencies to be found on the back end. ... Hanlon said he would expect management to look first at “facilities, technology, transmission and management overhead,” areas where CNN and CBS News could potentially reduce costs without changing who decides what gets covered. “Combining leases, vendors and technical infrastructure can produce real savings,” he said. ... International operations may offer the most obvious place to find larger savings. CNN has a broader international newsgathering footprint than CBS News, and the former senior TV news executive said it potentially gives CBS access to resources that now sit elsewhere inside the same company. The executive pointed specifically to bureaus, crews, producers, security, transmission and studio space — substantial expenses when wars, natural disasters or other breaking stories require journalists and equipment to be deployed quickly. In practice, that could mean combining some infrastructure while preserving separate editorial operations. CNN and CBS News could, for example, operate out of the same bureau space in a foreign city or use common transmission facilities or security resources while maintaining separate correspondents, producers and editorial chains. That could reduce some of the fixed costs of having two organizations in the same market without requiring the networks to make the same coverage decisions. ... Even the logistical side would vary by market. Employment laws, visas and press-accreditation requirements differ from country to country, the former senior TV news executive said, making some foreign operations easier to combine than others. The executive added that labor restrictions that could complicate domestic sharing would not necessarily apply in the same way overseas. ... Both CNN and CBS News have to fill hours of television and streaming programming each day. Two correspondents covering the same institution can look redundant on an organizational chart while still serving different shows, deadlines and editorial priorities. ... Skydance has so far kept the organizations’ leadership separate. Mark Thompson will remain chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss will continue as editor-in-chief of CBS News. The two executives make up Skydance’s “CEO News Executive Leadership Team” and report directly to Ellison and Kreiz. Skydance is also required to establish a five-member News Editorial Independence Board, which will set guiding editorial principles and handle certain disputes involving CNN and CBS News.

headline: Starbucks denies plan to buy Chipotle after report of possible takeover - CBS News
summary_text: # Starbucks denies plan to buy Chipotle after report of possible takeover By Megan Cerullo Megan Cerullo Reporter, MoneyWatch Megan Cerullo October 12, 2026 / 12:55 PM EDT / CBS News Starbucks shot down reports that the coffee giant was considering acquiring restaurant chain Chipotle Mexican Grill. A spokesperson for Starbucks said it is not buying Chipotle, which has a market worth of $47 billion, saying that the company is focused on its strategic plan to boost growth. "Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy. We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential. We look forward to sharing our Q4 results, including FY27 guidance, later this month," a Starbucks spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. Chipotle's stock soared as much as 8% last week after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been exploring a deal to purchase Chipotle. Industry analysts were skeptical of the report. TD Cowen analysts said in a research note last week that they considered a merger between Starbucks and Chipotle "a low-probability outcome," and instead expected Starbucks chief executive Brian Niccol to prioritize the company's turnaround plan. Niccol previously served as CEO of Chipotle, whose stock price has dropped about 50% since he left the post in August 2024. The shares have lost about 20% of their value over the past year.

headline: Chipotle shares jump after report that Starbucks has explored a takeover - CBS News
summary_text: Chipotle Mexican Grill's stock jumped as much as 8% on Thursday after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks has explored a deal to buy the "fast-casual" restaurant chain. A potential merger would represent one of the largest restaurant acquisitions in history, according to industry analysts. In 2014, Burger King acquired Canadian chain Tim Hortons in an $11.4 billion deal that remains one of the largest restaurant buyouts to date, according to Melius Research. Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol was previously chief executive of Chipotle, whose stock price has dropped about 50% since he left the post in August 2024. Its stock has lost about 20% of its value over the past year. Starbucks shares slipped about 4.4% in earlier trading on Thursday before recovering to end the day largely flat. Starbucks has recently sought counsel on a proposal to take over Chipotle, a $41 billion chain, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. It is unclear if Starbucks has made a formal offer to acquire the restaurant chain, the media outlet reported. "As a matter of policy, we don't comment on rumors and speculation," a Starbucks spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. "Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy. We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential." ... "Chipotle has struggled since Brian Niccol's departure and is pulling several levers to incentivize its customer base into visiting more often," analysts with Seaport Research Partners, an investor advisory firm, said in a report. "If synergies are not the primary motivation, then a key question for Brian Niccol would be what he would do differently than Chipotle's current management team." ... Chipotle's same-store sales dropped 2.5% in the fourth quarter of 2025, but rebounded in early 2026. The company reported revenue of $3.3 billion for the second quarter of 2026, up 9.3% compared to the year-ago period. The increase was driven by 100 new restaurant openings and growth in same-store sales, Chipotle said. ... "Starbucks' turnaround initiatives are beginning to deliver positive traffic, but U.S. operating margins remain pressured," Melius Research analysts said in a report. They added that Niccol's time at the helm of Chipotle gives him "considerable familiarity with the business he is reportedly considering acquiring." Still, Wall Street analysts said there are no obvious synergies between the two companies, while TD Cowen analysts said they view the deal "as a low-probability outcome at this stage." "We argue Brian Niccol's priority at Starbucks has been executing the 'Back to Starbucks' U.S. turnaround," and pursuing a $40 billion acquisition would seem "inconsistent" with that goal, TD Cowen said.

headline: Paramount closes $110 billion deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, creating Skydance - CBS News
summary_text: # Paramount closes $110 billion deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, creating Skydance By Mary Cunningham Mary Cunningham Reporter, MoneyWatch Mary Cunningham Updated on: October 6, 2026 / 8:38 PM EDT / CBS News Paramount Skydance on Tuesday completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, uniting the movie studios behind "The Godfather" and the "Harry Potter" films into a media colossus rebranded as Skydance. The merger also brings together the news outlets CBS News and CNN, major cable networks such as Comedy Central, Nickelodeon, TBS and TNT and the streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max. David Ellison, who orchestrated the merger as CEO of Paramount Skydance, will lead the new company along with co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, who was previously CEO of toy company Mattel. In an email to employees, Ellison and Kreiz said the merger will allow the company to create a "stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry." "Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a separate statement from Skydance. ... As part of the deal, Warner Bros. shareholders will receive the cash equivalent of roughly $31 per share, the company said. The deal came together after Paramount settled a July lawsuit from a coalition of 12 state attorneys general and a separate lawsuit from the Writers Guild of America (WGA). Both had sued to block it on antitrust grounds. Under the settlement agreement, Paramount pledged to produce 30 films in each of the first two years after the merger and is barred from selling or closing the Paramount or Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles for at least five years. Paramount has also agreed to establish an editorial board to "help CNN and CBS maintain editorial independence," according to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office. WGA agreed to settle its lawsuit after Paramount reached a deal with the states. Ellison and Kreiz said the company is targeting $6 billion in cost savings, a move that some in the media industry are concerned could lead to job losses. "Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce," the co-CEOs said in the email to Skydance employees.
